newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HOODOO GURUS PLANNING FAREWELL TOUR
After 16 years together Australian band, the Hoodoo Gurus, has decided to split up.
The band will embark on their final overseas tour to Brazil next week before arranging a farewell Australia tour.
The Gurus say they won't be making any new studio albums.
JAZZ MUSIC A TURN-ON FOR PIGS
Pigs in a New South Wales piggery are being played jazz music to "get them in the mood".
Management at the Parkville piggery in the upper hunter say the pigs' mating behaviour improved when a member of staff put a stereo near one of the pens.
They say while it appears the pigs prefer rock music, jazz creates a more romantic atmosphere and has led to increased mating.
For the less sexually inclined pigs, management is considering buying them soccer balls to occupy their time.
INTERNET PROVIDERS CONDEMN TELSTRA MOVES
Moves by Telstra to charge Internet users for incoming data calls have been condemned by Internet service providers.
The Internet Society of Australia's Simon Hackett says if the moves aren't blocked, many service providers would go out of business.
A senate committee has heard Telstra wants time-based charges for internet calls levied at the receiving end, because it fears internet users may soon over load the telephone network.
The Communcations Minister has guaranteed internet users continued access to untimed local calls to their service providers.
But service providers say there's nothing in the bill to stop Telstra also time-charging Internet Service Providers, when users "go on line".
OUTRAGE OVER PUBLICATION OF PAEDOPHILES NAMES

A civil liberties activist says the Australian Press Council isn't doing its job if it fails to take action over the publication of names of sex offenders and paedophiles in a North Queensland newspaper.
Yesterday the Townsville Bulletin re-produced eight local offender's names, ages, and criminal details from the controversial Australian Paedophile and Sex Offender Index.
National Civil Liberties President, Terry O'Gorman says the Press Council will be worthless as a media regulator if it fails to censor the article.
Mr O'Gorman says the Townsville Bulletin has dropped to the lowest level of tabloid journalism he's ever seen.
He says the effect of the publication on the families of victims, and the offenders families is going to be horrendous.
CALL FOR NEW SCHEME FOR AUSTUDY ACCESSMENT
Students say the means test accessment method for Austudy needs to be eliminated and a new scheme adopted.
The Federal Government's planning to re-access thousands of Austudy applications, after it was found some who deserved financial support were ineligible under the means test.
The National Union of Students says that instead of tinkering with the test, the government should totally overhaul it.
Employment, Education and Training minister, Amanda Vanstone, has apologised to students for the unnecessarily bureaucratic management of scheme.
Senator Vanstone concedes the system was too harsh and some students entitled to Austudy may have been disadvantaged.
THREE MINERS INJURED OVERNIGHT
Three miners have been hurt in accidents at Hunter Valley coal mines overnight.
A man is being treated by paramedics underground after being injured in a rock fall at the Gretley colliery in Newcastle.
He's suffered leg injuries in the accident, which happened 15 kilometres from the mine entrance. A man was crushed by machinery at the Hunter Valley number one mine near Singleton last night.
He was flown by rescue helicopter to Newcastle's John Hunter Hospital with a fractured pelvis and leg injuries.
And a 27 year old man was hurt in a rock fall at the Cooranbong Colliery, south of Newcastle.
He suffered head and neck injuries and was taken by rescue helicopter to the John Hunter Hospital in a stable condition.
NUCLEAR WASTE SHIP HEADING TOWARDS TASMANIA - GREENPEACE
Greenpeace believes a ship carrying nuclear waste to Japan is near South Australia and heading towards Tasmania.
The environmental group has been doing aerial checks to try to find it.
Tasmania's Environment Minister Peter Hodgman will raise the issue at a meeting of environment ministers in Canberra today.
But he says he understands the Commonwealth's reluctance to say where the ship is.
Mr Hodgman says the Federal Government probably doesn't want to alarm people unnecessarily by disclosing the location.
